records.name: Map Lichen
records.diet: Makes its own food: the algal partner inside it photosynthesises, while the fungal partner grips the rock and traps water and dust
records.shelter: None — it is the crust itself, welded to bare, stable rock
records.preferredHabitat: Exposed, undisturbed boulders, talus and scree above treeline, especially north-facing rock
records.fact: Map lichen grows about a millimetre every ten years, so a patch the size of your palm can be older than the town at the bottom of the mountain.
records.role: One of the two organisms that start alpine soil. Crustose lichens etch and crumble bare rock, and the dust and dead lichen they leave behind fills the cracks that cushion plants later root in. Pikas and deer nibble it, and the mineral grit it makes is the base of everything else in the biome.
eatsOther: dust blown in on the wind

requirements.hint: Stable, undisturbed rock and clean air — nothing else. Set the boulders where nobody will walk, because at a millimetre a decade this is the slowest thing you will ever grow.

sources.name: Aston Research Explorer — The biology of the crustose lichen Rhizocarpon geographicum
Bradwell & Armstrong — Growth rates of Rhizocarpon geographicum lichens

records.name: Moss Campion
records.diet: Makes its own food by photosynthesis; roots reach deep into gravel for water and the few nutrients up here
records.shelter: None — the cushion is its own shelter, trapping heat and moisture around its stems
records.preferredHabitat: Fellfields and frost-heaved gravel flats above treeline, and stable talus edges
records.fact: Inside a moss campion cushion the air can sit up to 10 C warmer than the wind just above it, which is why seedlings of other alpine plants so often start life inside one.
records.role: A cushion plant and the second of the biome's two producers. It grows only a few millimetres a year, takes many years to flower for the first time, and builds soil and shelter as it spreads. Bumble bees and butterflies feed at its flowers; pikas, marmots and ptarmigan graze it; and its dead stems are the litter the decomposers work on.

requirements.hint: Open, wind-scoured gravel that freezes and heaves — no shade, no rich soil, no water feature. Cushion plants want the hardest ground on the mountain, and decades to fill it.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service — Moss Campion (Silene acaulis)
NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Silene acaulis

records.name: Snow Flea
records.diet: Dead leaves and stems, fungal threads, pollen and the algae that grow on old snow
records.shelter: Damp litter, moss cushions and the gaps in alpine soil; in winter, the space between the snowpack and the ground
records.preferredHabitat: Moist alpine turf, moss cushions and snowmelt litter, and the surface of late-lying snow on warm days
records.fact: Snow fleas carry a glycine-rich antifreeze protein that lets them stay active below freezing, which is why they turn up in their thousands on the snow on a mild day.
records.role: A springtail, and the animal end of decomposition up here. It shreds dead plant material and grazes fungal threads, turning last year's stems into soil, and it stays working through the winter under the snow. Pipits, sparrows, rosy-finches, chickadees, bluebirds and toads all eat it.

requirements.hint: Damp litter and moss, not open water. Springtails drink through their skin from wet leaf mould, so what they need is ground that never quite dries out.

records.name: Snowbank Fuzzy Foot
records.diet: Digests well-rotted conifer wood, releasing its nutrients back into the soil
records.shelter: Threads growing through soft, wet, decaying logs and stumps beneath the snowpack
records.preferredHabitat: Rotting fir and pine logs at the treeline forest edge, where snowdrifts lie latest
records.fact: This mushroom does its growing under the snow at temperatures near freezing, then fruits in clusters right at the edge of the melting drift.
records.role: A wood-rotting fungus and the biome's true decomposer, breaking dead trees down into nutrients that living plants can use again. Alpine decomposition is slow and mostly happens in winter under the snow, which is a large part of why a damaged slope up here takes so long to recover. Springtails and chipmunks feed on it.

requirements.hint: Dead wood is habitat. Leave a well-rotted fir log where deep drifts pile up against the last trees — that damp, buried wood is the fungus's whole world.

sources.name: Snowbank fungus — ecology of the snowbank fungal group

records.name: Bighorn Sheep
records.diet: Chiefly grasses and sedges, with forbs and woody browse in winter
records.shelter: Beds on rocky ledges and rugged escape terrain near cliffs
records.preferredHabitat: Open alpine turf directly beside steep, broken escape cliffs
records.fact: Bighorns flee across rocky ledges barely a few inches wide to escape predators.
records.role: A cliff-edge grazer that crops turf on open slopes and never feeds far from broken cliff it can climb into. Rams clash horns in booming rutting contests each fall. Mountain lions are the main predator of adults and lambs; golden eagles take newborn lambs from ledges.

requirements.hint: Good grazing is only half of it. Bighorns will not use a slope they cannot escape from, so put the turf right against broken cliff.

records.name: American Pika
records.diet: Grasses, forbs, wildflowers and lichen, cut green and dried into winter haypiles
records.shelter: Cool gaps deep within talus and broken rock
records.preferredHabitat: Deep, stable talus with alpine flower turf right at its edge
records.fact: Pikas cut and sun-dry little haystacks of plants, then eat from them under the snow all winter.
records.role: A tiny talus-dwelling relative of rabbits and one of the best sentinel species for a warming climate — pikas overheat easily and have been lost from lower, hotter talus. It spends the whole summer haying. Weasels, martens, foxes and eagles all hunt it.

requirements.hint: Deep talus to hide in and flowers within a short dash of it — then a haypile, because a pika that cannot cure hay in summer will not survive the winter. Pikas drink almost nothing; their water comes from the plants they eat.

records.name: Yellow-bellied Marmot
records.diet: Grasses, flowering plants and seeds, eaten hard through a short summer
records.shelter: Deep, many-chambered burrows dug beneath boulders, below the frost line
records.preferredHabitat: Open alpine turf broken by boulders, with diggable soil underneath
records.fact: A marmot sleeps about eight months of the year and can lose half its body weight before it wakes.
records.role: A stout, sun-loving rodent that grazes meadow plants and fattens fast before an eight-month hibernation. Colonies whistle alarm calls from boulder lookouts. Its abandoned burrows become homes for foxes, bumble bee queens and toads, which makes it an ecosystem engineer as well as prey for eagles, foxes and martens.

requirements.hint: Soil deep enough to dig, a boulder to dig under and a lot of green forage close by. Do not look for marmots after early autumn — they are underground until spring.

records.name: Snowshoe Hare
records.diet: Green plants in summer; willow and juniper twigs, buds, bark and conifer needles in winter
records.shelter: Shallow 'forms' scraped under dense shrubs and low conifer branches
records.preferredHabitat: Dense krummholz, juniper and willow thickets at and just below treeline
records.fact: Its molt from brown to winter white is triggered by day length, not by snow — so an early thaw can leave a white hare on brown ground.
records.role: A browsing hare of thick treeline cover whose coat flips brown-to-white with the seasons. Its famous ten-year population cycle is a northern boreal pattern; in southern mountains like these the swings are much softer. Cover is everything to it — martens, foxes, eagles and mountain lions all hunt it.

requirements.hint: Thick, low, tangled cover it can freeze motionless inside — and willow to browse in winter. Open ground with a rock pile on it is the opposite of hare habitat. It eats snow instead of drinking.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service FEIS — Lepus americanus

records.name: Mule Deer
records.diet: A selective browser of shrubs, forbs, buds, fruits and lichens
records.shelter: Day beds in shaded, wind-broken hollows under krummholz
records.preferredHabitat: High summer basins with willow browse and clean water, abandoned for lower ground each autumn
records.fact: When a mule deer bounds away it releases scent from a gland on its hind leg that warns other deer of danger.
records.role: A selective high-country browser that summers in alpine basins and shrublands and migrates down the mountain each fall. It picks the most digestible forbs, buds and browse, and its browsing shapes the willow. Mountain lions are its main predator; golden eagles take newborn fawns.

requirements.hint: Browse, shade to lie up in through the day, and clean water. Mule deer are only here for the warm months — they walk down the mountain before the snow closes it.

records.name: White-tailed Ptarmigan
records.diet: Buds, twigs, leaves, seeds and flowers; in winter almost entirely willow buds and twigs
records.shelter: Camouflaged ground scrapes among lichen-covered rock, and burrows dug into soft snow to roost
records.preferredHabitat: Alpine tundra above treeline year-round, dropping into sheltered willow basins in winter
records.fact: It is the only North American bird that spends its whole life cycle in alpine habitat — it drops below the tundra only into sheltered willow basins in the worst storms.
records.role: A superbly camouflaged alpine grouse that grazes buds, leaves and seeds and survives winter almost entirely on willow. It grows feathered 'snowshoes' on its feet and burrows into snowdrifts to roost out of the wind. Eagles, foxes, weasels and martens all hunt it and its chicks.

requirements.hint: Willow is the whole winter for a ptarmigan, and a soft drift to burrow into is where it sleeps out a storm. It eats snow rather than drinking, and it does not need a flower planter.

sources.name: All About Birds — White-tailed Ptarmigan life history

records.name: Rocky Mountain Parnassian
records.diet: Caterpillars eat lance-leaved stonecrop and nothing else; adults sip nectar from alpine flowers
records.shelter: No nest — the caterpillar develops fully inside the egg and overwinters there, hatching at snowmelt
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky open alpine and subalpine slopes where stonecrop grows between the stones
records.fact: Its wings are almost see-through white, and the red spots on them warn birds that it tastes foul.
records.role: A hardy alpine butterfly whose caterpillars will eat one plant and one plant only, so where the stonecrop goes the butterfly goes. Adults nectar across the meadow flowers. Its warning colours put most birds off, though not all of them.

requirements.hint: Nectar for the adults, but stonecrop for the caterpillars — plant flowers without the host plant and you get visitors, not a population.

sources.name: Butterflies and Moths of North America — Parnassius smintheus

records.name: High Country Bumble Bee
records.diet: Nectar and pollen from deep-throated alpine flowers such as gentian and clover
records.shelter: Colonies in abandoned rodent burrows, insulated with dry grass
records.preferredHabitat: High alpine flower meadows above treeline, with old rodent holes to nest in
records.fact: Between the 1960s and today this bee's tongue has grown measurably shorter as the deep alpine flowers it fed on have declined.
records.role: A cold-tolerant, long-tongued bumble bee that pollinates deep alpine blossoms, shivering its flight muscles to fly in near-freezing air. A queen cannot dig, so she has to find an abandoned rodent burrow — losing the burrowers means losing the bees. Birds and crab spiders take foragers.

requirements.hint: Flowers are only half of what a bumble bee needs. The other half is a hole in the ground somebody else dug — bring the marmots back first.

sources.name: Miller-Struttmann et al., tongue length in alpine bumble bees

records.name: Least Chipmunk
records.diet: Seeds of grasses, sedges and forbs, plus berries, fungi, insects and the occasional bird egg
records.shelter: Burrows and nests packed into crevices between talus rocks and under slabs
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky alpine turf and krummholz edges, from sagebrush country right up onto the tundra
records.fact: A least chipmunk does not fatten up for winter the way a marmot does — it sleeps in short stretches and wakes to eat from the larder it buried.
records.role: A small, wide-ranging seed-eater that caches seeds and so helps replant alpine plants across the talus. It also eats fungi and insects and raids the nests of ground-nesting songbirds, which makes it an omnivore rather than a plant-eater. Foxes, weasels, martens and eagles all hunt it, and its old burrows shelter toads and weasels.

requirements.hint: Rock to nest in, seed plants to harvest, and somewhere dry to bury the harvest. It sleeps out most of the winter, so look for it in the warm months.

records.name: Clark's Nutcracker
records.diet: Whitebark and limber pine seeds cached by the thousand, plus insects and small animals
records.shelter: Cup nest in a conifer, sited near the winter seed caches
records.preferredHabitat: Treeline conifer forest and krummholz within reach of pine-seed sources
records.fact: It can relocate thousands of buried seed caches months later, even under snow.
records.role: A mountain corvid locked in a partnership with whitebark pine: the tree's cones do not open on their own, so almost every whitebark seedling on the mountain grew from a seed a nutcracker buried and forgot. Its cached hoard lets it breed in deep winter. It also takes insects and small animals.

requirements.hint: A nutcracker needs a seed bank it can find again under the snow. Build the caches, and the pines it plants will follow.

sources.name: All About Birds — Clark's Nutcracker life history

records.name: Gray-crowned Rosy-Finch
records.diet: Tiny alpine plant seeds and insects, often gleaned off the surface of snowfields
records.shelter: Bulky cup of moss and grass wedged deep into a cliff crack or a hole in talus
records.preferredHabitat: Above treeline: talus, scree, cliff faces and the edges of permanent snow
records.fact: It nests higher than nearly any other songbird in North America, deep inside cracks in cliffs and rockslides.
records.role: A high-altitude songbird that hops across snow and talus gathering wind-blown seeds and chilled insects. It is an obligate crevice nester — without deep cracks in rock it simply cannot breed here. Golden eagles and weasels take it.

requirements.hint: Rock with real cracks in it, not a pile of stones. A rosy-finch nests inside the cliff, forages across the scree, and drinks from snowmelt.

sources.name: All About Birds — Gray-crowned Rosy-Finch life history

records.name: White-crowned Sparrow
records.diet: Mainly seeds, plus caterpillars, beetles, springtails and bees in summer
records.shelter: Cup nest on the ground or low in dwarf heath, hidden among moss and lichen
records.preferredHabitat: Krummholz edges and alpine heath with patches of bare ground to forage on
records.fact: Young white-crowns learn their song dialect from the neighbours nearby, so birds a valley apart can sound different.
records.role: A ground-foraging sparrow of alpine heath and krummholz edges that eats seeds and switches to insects to feed its chicks. It disperses seeds and moves energy from the insect layer up to the predators. Foxes, weasels and martens hunt the adults and raid its low nests.

requirements.hint: It builds on the ground in low heath, not on a ledge. Give it a heather mat to hide the nest in and krummholz to sing from.

sources.name: All About Birds — White-crowned Sparrow life history

records.name: American Pipit
records.diet: Mostly insects, springtails, spiders and their larvae, plus some seeds
records.shelter: Ground nest of grass tucked into the turf beside a rock or a tussock
records.preferredHabitat: Open alpine turf and fellfield, especially along the edges of melting snow
records.fact: It works the edge of a melting snowfield for insects that were carried up the mountain by the wind and knocked flat by the cold.
records.role: A slender ground-walking songbird of open alpine turf that constantly bobs its tail as it hunts. It feeds heavily on the wind-delivered insect fallout stranded on snowfields, which is one of the strangest food subsidies in the mountains. Foxes and weasels take it and its ground nests.

requirements.hint: Open turf to walk and nest in, and a lingering snowbank with a dark debris line at its edge — that stripe of stranded insects is the pipit's dinner table.

sources.name: Birds of the World — American Pipit food habits

records.name: Boreal Toad
records.diet: Beetles, ants, flies, springtails and other invertebrates; tadpoles graze algae
records.shelter: Rodent burrows, rock chambers and damp cover above the breeding pools
records.preferredHabitat: Subalpine and alpine wet meadows with shallow, sun-warmed, fish-free breeding pools
records.fact: A boreal toad spends September to May underground, then breeds in pools that were solid ice a few weeks earlier.
records.role: The high country's only toad, an insect-eater that breeds in shallow snowmelt pools and takes years to mature. Its tadpoles graze algae and are eaten by almost nothing here — its skin toxins put off the foxes and weasels, so its real threats are chytrid fungus and stocked trout, not predators. The Southern Rocky Mountain population is a conservation flagship.

requirements.hint: Shallow warm pools to breed in, and a burrow to spend the other eight months of the year in. Keep the pools fishless — stocked trout are the single biggest reason alpine amphibians disappear.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service FEIS — Anaxyrus boreas
NPS Rocky Mountain NP — Where do boreal toads spend the winter?
Colorado Parks and Wildlife — Boreal Toad

records.name: Mountain Bluebird
records.diet: Mostly insects taken in flight or dropped on from a perch; berries and seeds in colder months
records.shelter: Old woodpecker holes and other ready-made cavities — it cannot make its own
records.preferredHabitat: Open high meadows and burned or beetle-killed edges with scattered dead trees to nest in
records.fact: It cannot dig its own hole, so every bluebird nest you ever see was made by a woodpecker, or by a person copying one.
records.role: A brilliant sky-blue thrush of open high meadows that hovers and drops on insects in the turf below. Because it is a secondary cavity nester, its numbers are set by how many old woodpecker holes are standing — no snags, no bluebirds, however much food there is. Martens and weasels raid its cavities.

requirements.hint: Open turf to hunt over and a hole it did not make. A bluebird can starve beside a full meadow if there is no old woodpecker cavity to nest in.

records.name: Mountain Chickadee
records.diet: Insects, spiders and bark-beetle larvae in summer; cached conifer seeds in fall and winter
records.shelter: Existing cavities in dead conifers — old woodpecker holes, or soft rotten wood it can enlarge
records.preferredHabitat: Treeline conifer forest of fir and whitebark pine with standing dead trees
records.fact: It caches thousands of seeds one at a time and remembers where it hid them months later.
records.role: A busy conifer-forest insectivore that gleans insects and beetle larvae from bark and twigs and switches to cached seeds in winter. It is the nucleus of mixed foraging flocks and helps disperse conifer seeds. It needs dead wood: it can only enlarge a cavity where the wood is already soft. Weasels, foxes and martens take it and its nestlings.

requirements.hint: Dead trees are not waste — a beetle-killed snag is both the chickadee's larder and the only wood soft enough for it to nest in. The whitebark pines come from the nutcracker's forgotten caches.

sources.name: All About Birds — Mountain Chickadee life history

records.name: Red Fox
records.diet: Voles, pikas, hares, ground birds and eggs, insects and berries
records.shelter: Earthen dens, usually burrows taken over from marmots or other diggers
records.preferredHabitat: High country with talus, diggable ground and abundant small prey
records.fact: Red foxes rarely dig their own den if somebody else has already done the work — most alpine fox dens started as marmot burrows.
records.role: An adaptable mountain mesopredator that hunts pikas, marmots, hares and ground birds and rounds its diet out with insects and berries. It listens for prey moving beneath the snow, then dives in headfirst. Golden eagles take its kits.

requirements.hint: Foxes follow the pikas and marmots — and they move into the marmots' old burrows rather than dig their own.

records.name: American Marten
records.diet: Voles, red squirrels, pikas, hares, birds, eggs, insects and berries
records.shelter: Dens in hollow logs, tree cavities and rock crevices, usually under deep snow
records.preferredHabitat: Structurally complex treeline forest with big trees, dead wood and rock
records.fact: Martens hunt beneath the winter snowpack, in tunnels between the snow and the ground that no other predator its size can use.
records.role: An agile treeline weasel that hunts voles, pikas and young hares and adds berries and insects in season. It needs structure above all — big conifers, hollow logs and rock — which is why logging and clearing hit it so hard. Golden eagles take it.

requirements.hint: You cannot build marten habitat out of rocks and flowers. It needs a stand of real trees, dead wood on the ground, and hares and pikas already living there.

sources.name: Alaska Department of Fish and Game — American marten

records.name: American Ermine
records.diet: Small rodents, especially voles; also young pikas, birds, eggs and insects
records.shelter: Dens taken over from its prey — rodent burrows and rock crevices, relined with the previous owner's fur
records.preferredHabitat: Talus and heath edges beside turf with dense rodent prey, used all year round
records.fact: Its coat turns pure white in winter except for a jet-black tail tip — but the animal itself does not disappear in summer; it is here in every season.
records.role: A small, fierce weasel that specialises in voles and other rodents and also takes young pikas, nestlings and eggs. Long and thin enough to hunt inside its prey's own tunnels, it stays active and resident year-round rather than hibernating. Foxes, martens and eagles kill it in turn.

requirements.hint: An ermine does not build — it moves into a burrow it has just emptied. Bring the chipmunks and pikas back first. You can find it in any season, not only winter.

sources.name: Idaho Fish and Game species catalog — ermine

records.name: Golden Eagle
records.diet: Marmots, hares, ground squirrels, ptarmigan and other birds, plus carrion
records.shelter: Huge stick eyries built on sheer cliff ledges and reused for decades
records.preferredHabitat: Open, high country with big cliffs to nest on and plenty of medium-sized prey
records.fact: Golden eagles sometimes line their nests with fresh aromatic leaves, which may help keep insects down.
records.role: The airborne apex hunter of the high country, taking marmots, hares and ptarmigan and even smaller carnivores in powerful stoops. It takes newborn lambs, fawns and fox kits, but not adult sheep or deer. It arrives only when the mountain teems with prey, and adults have essentially no predators.

requirements.hint: Eagles arrive last — when the high country is truly alive again. They need a real cliff to build the eyrie on and open ground below to hunt over.

sources.name: All About Birds — Golden Eagle life history
Birds of the World — Golden Eagle food habits

records.name: Mountain Lion
records.diet: Mainly mule deer, plus bighorn sheep, marmots and hares
records.shelter: Kittens are raised in a dry overhang or rock cave deep in broken cliff; adults have no fixed den
records.preferredHabitat: Rugged broken terrain with cover to stalk through, from the subalpine forest up onto the tundra edge
records.fact: A mountain lion drags a large kill under cover and buries it in needles and snow, then returns to feed on it for several days.
records.role: The mammal apex predator of the Southern Rockies and the reason the ungulates here are not unregulated. Hunting by ambush rather than pursuit, it needs rugged ground and cover, and it kills mule deer above everything else. Its half-eaten, cached kills are also the main source of winter carrion for smaller scavengers. Adults have no predators.

requirements.hint: A lion needs deer before it needs anything else, then broken ground it can stalk through and a sheltered ledge to raise kittens on. It is the last animal to come back.

sources.name: Colorado Parks and Wildlife — Mountain Lion

records.name: Giant Kelp
records.diet: Makes its own food from sunlight and dissolved nutrients carried in by cold upwelled water
records.shelter: Anchors to rock with a root-like holdfast; gas-filled floats lift the blades to the surface
records.preferredHabitat: Cool, clear, nutrient-rich water over rocky bottom, roughly 5-25 m deep
records.fact: Giant kelp can grow up to about 60 cm in a single day, making it one of the fastest-growing living things on Earth.
records.role: The primary producer this whole coast is built on. Its canopy feeds sea urchins directly, sheds drift kelp that feeds the wrack line, and forms the three-dimensional forest that otters raft in and small fish shelter in. Everything above it in the food web ultimately traces back to kelp and sunlight.

requirements.hint: Kelp is not a plant that grows in sand — it needs bare rock to grip and cold, nutrient-rich water above it.

records.name: Torrey's Surfgrass
records.diet: Photosynthesises in the surf zone; takes nutrients up through roots anchored in rock
records.shelter: Tough rhizomes gripping wave-scoured rock in the low intertidal
records.preferredHabitat: Wave-swept low intertidal rock, often fringing the seaward edge of tidepools
records.fact: Surfgrass is a true flowering plant, not a seaweed — and its seeds carry two bristly arms that hook onto branching red and coralline algae until the seedling can root on the rock.
records.role: The rocky shore's flowering plant and a foundation species of the low zone. Its meadows shade and cool the rock at low tide, trap sediment, and shelter a dense community of small invertebrates and juvenile fish. It is a second, independent base to the food web alongside kelp.

requirements.hint: Surfgrass seeds cannot grab bare stone. Grow the branching coralline turf first — the seeds hook onto it.

sources.name: Blanchette et al., Mar Ecol Prog Ser 184: Recruitment of surfgrass Phyllospadix torreyi

records.name: Purple Sea Urchin
records.diet: Living kelp and surfgrass, drift kelp, and encrusting coralline algae
records.shelter: Pits it grinds into the rock itself with its teeth and spines
records.preferredHabitat: Wave-exposed low intertidal and shallow subtidal rock near kelp
records.fact: Purple urchins slowly grind pits into solid rock and sit in them for years — on some reefs urchins erode more rock than the waves do.
records.role: The grazer in the middle of this coast's most famous story. Fed on drift kelp and controlled by sea otters, urchins are one part of a healthy kelp forest. Released from predation they mow the kelp down to bare rock — an urchin barren — and the forest, and everything living in it, goes with it.

requirements.hint: Urchins need kelp to eat before they can live here — and once they are here, they need a predator, or they will eat all of it.

records.name: Northern Anchovy
records.diet: Plankton — copepods, diatoms and larvae — strained from the water or picked one at a time
records.shelter: The school itself; open nearshore water, with kelp and surfgrass edges as nursery cover
records.preferredHabitat: Cool, plankton-rich nearshore water over the shelf
records.fact: An anchovy can switch between snapping at single prey and swimming open-mouthed to filter plankton out of the water, depending on how big the food is.
records.role: The forage fish that carries plankton energy up to everything with a beak or teeth. Pelicans, guillemots and harbour seals all live or fail on anchovy schools, and California brown pelican colonies are abandoned in years when the anchovies do not show up.

requirements.hint: Anchovies need open water with plankton in it — cold upwelling first, then quiet shallows to spawn in.

records.name: California Beach Hopper
records.diet: Decaying kelp and other stranded seaweed in the wrack line
records.shelter: Burrows dug in damp sand high on the beach, and the damp underside of drift kelp and driftwood
records.preferredHabitat: Gently sloping sandy beach with an undisturbed wrack line
records.fact: Beach hoppers spend the day sealed in a burrow high up the dry beach and come out after dark to shred the seaweed the tide left behind.
records.role: The engine of the beach's decomposition. Hoppers break stranded kelp down into fragments and nutrients that feed the sand community, and in doing so they convert dead seaweed into the shorebird food that plovers, sanderlings and gulls come to the tide line for. Groom the wrack away and this link disappears.

requirements.hint: No water needed — hoppers live above the tide. They need the wrack left where it lands and dry sand to burrow in.

sources.name: California Conservation Genomics Project — Megalorchestia californiana

records.name: Blueband Hermit Crab
records.diet: Algae, detritus, and scavenged carrion
records.shelter: Borrowed empty snail shells
records.preferredHabitat: Tidepools and low rock benches with a supply of empty snail shells
records.fact: When one hermit crab moves into a bigger shell, a smaller crab takes the shell it left behind — and so on down a chain.
records.role: A tidepool detritivore that grazes algae and cleans up carrion, and one of the shore's recyclers: the empty shells it depends on are the leftovers of dead snails. Shell supply, not food, is usually what limits how many hermit crabs a shore can hold. It is common prey for gulls and turnstones.

requirements.hint: Tidepools are not enough — a hermit crab cannot live without a supply of empty snail shells to move into.

records.name: Bat Star
records.diet: Algae, detritus, and dead plants and animals
records.shelter: Rocky rubble bottoms, surfgrass beds and kelp holdfasts
records.preferredHabitat: Shallow rocky and rubble bottom with surfgrass or kelp
records.fact: A bat star can have anywhere from four to nine arms, not always five.
records.role: The cleanup crew of the shallows. It slides its stomach out over the seafloor and digests algae, detritus and dead animals where they lie, recycling material that would otherwise sit there. Its work is the same job a fungus or an earthworm does on land.

requirements.hint: Rubble bottom with surfgrass over it — bat stars are rocky-bottom animals, not eelgrass animals.

records.name: California Mussel
records.diet: Plankton filtered from seawater
records.shelter: Dense beds anchored to wave-washed rock by byssal threads
records.preferredHabitat: Exposed rocky shore with clean, constantly moving water
records.fact: A mussel holds onto the rock with byssal threads it spins from a gland in its foot — and it can cut them and crawl a short way to a better spot.
records.role: A reef-building filter feeder whose beds are habitat in their own right, with hundreds of small animals living in the spaces between shells. It is the key prey that ties this shore's predators together — ochre sea stars, oystercatchers and sea otters all depend on it.

requirements.hint: A filter feeder needs water that moves. Give it surge-washed rock, not a still pool — and barnacle crust for its larvae to settle on.

records.name: Pacific Littleneck Clam
records.diet: Plankton filtered from seawater
records.shelter: Buried a few centimetres down in sand and gravel
records.preferredHabitat: Stable sand-and-gravel of protected bays and low intertidal flats
records.fact: The rings on a littleneck's shell record its good and bad seasons — storms, spawning and cold snaps all leave a mark, and biologists read them to estimate its age.
records.role: A buried filter feeder that helps clean coastal water and stores energy in sheltered sediment. It is important prey for sea otters and gulls, which dig it up or crack it open.

requirements.hint: Not a tidepool animal — littlenecks bury in the stable sand and gravel of a sheltered bay.

records.name: Gray Whale
records.diet: Bottom-living amphipods and swarming mysid shrimp, sifted through baleen
records.shelter: Open ocean; passes close inshore along a healthy coast
records.preferredHabitat: Nearshore water with soft-bottom amphipod beds and mysid swarms at the kelp edge
records.fact: Gray whales migrate up to 14,000 miles round trip, among the longest journeys of any mammal.
records.role: A bottom-feeding baleen whale that rolls onto its side and sucks up sediment to strain out small crustaceans — it is not a plankton skimmer. Along this coast it feeds on mysid swarms held by kelp beds, so a whale lingering offshore is a direct readout of how the kelp forest is doing.

requirements.hint: A whale needs open ocean and something to eat in it. Tidepools and dune plantings will never bring one in.

sources.name: Hildebrand et al. 2024, Sci Rep — urchin/kelp cascade and gray whale foraging

records.name: Black Brant
records.diet: Eelgrass, plus sea lettuce and other green algae
records.shelter: Open shoreline, sandbars and shallow bays
records.preferredHabitat: Shallow coastal bays with eelgrass beds
records.fact: Whole flocks of brant time their migration to the eelgrass beds along this coast, and a bay that loses its eelgrass loses its brant within a season or two.
records.role: A small sea goose that grazes almost entirely on eelgrass and green algae in shallow bays. Its dependence on eelgrass makes healthy brant flocks a clear indicator of intact seagrass beds.

requirements.hint: Eelgrass to graze and a quiet sandbar to rest on between tides.

records.name: Purple Shore Crab
records.diet: Sea lettuce and other green algae scraped from rock, plus occasional carrion
records.shelter: The undersides of loose cobbles in the sheltered intertidal
records.preferredHabitat: Sheltered mid-to-high intertidal cobble and stone
records.fact: Turn over a loose stone on a sheltered shore and purple shore crabs scatter — they spend low tide pressed to the damp underside of it.
records.role: A grazing crab that scrapes algae from intertidal rocks and moves that plant energy up the food web. It is common prey for gulls, anemones and turnstones, and it needs loose rock it can hide under, not open reef.

requirements.hint: Loose cobbles it can crawl under, on a shore the surf does not pound.

records.name: Striped Shore Crab
records.diet: Mostly algae and drift kelp, plus detritus, worms, snails and carrion
records.shelter: Crevices in splash-zone rock
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky intertidal and splash zone, often out of the water altogether
records.fact: The striped shore crab is semi-terrestrial: it spends more than half its time out of the water and can breathe air, returning to a pool now and then to wet its gills.
records.role: An abundant grazer-scavenger of the highest rocks that keeps surfaces clear of algae and recycles carrion. It is a key prey item for gulls, oystercatchers and turnstones, and one of the first animals to come back to a recovering shore.

requirements.hint: Only a little water — this crab lives mostly above the tide and breathes air, but it needs a pool to duck into.

records.name: Western Gull
records.diet: Fish, crabs, clams, sea stars and carrion
records.shelter: Ground scrapes on offshore rocks and islands, tucked beside driftwood, rock or low coastal scrub
records.preferredHabitat: Any shoreline with food to scavenge or catch
records.fact: Western gulls carry clams and crabs high into the air and drop them onto rock to crack them open — and will go back to the same reliable rock again and again.
records.role: A bold generalist that scavenges carrion and preys on crabs, shellfish, anchovies and even sea stars, cleaning the beach and linking many prey to the top of the food web. On this roster nothing preys on the adult gull.

requirements.hint: Open beach to patrol, low scrub to nest beside, and a hard rock to drop shellfish onto.

records.name: Sanderling
records.diet: Beach hoppers, mole crabs, amphipods, worms and small molluscs
records.shelter: Open beach above the surf line
records.preferredHabitat: The wet swash zone of an open sandy beach
records.fact: Sanderlings chase retreating waves in busy little sprints to grab invertebrates before the next wave buries them again.
records.role: A swash-zone specialist that feeds on small crustaceans churned up by the surf. Its winter flocks track the health of open sandy beaches, and it depends directly on the beach hoppers and mole crabs the wrack line produces.

requirements.hint: The wet strip where the waves run out, and open sand behind it — no grass, that is not where a sanderling feeds.

records.name: Western Snowy Plover
records.diet: Beach invertebrates: beach hoppers, kelp flies and their larvae, small crustaceans and molluscs
records.shelter: A shallow scrape on open sand, sometimes lined with shell fragments; chicks shelter beside driftwood and wrack
records.preferredHabitat: Wide, flat, sparsely vegetated open sand above the tide line
records.fact: A snowy plover's nest is just a scrape in bare sand — which is why dense beachgrass is removed from recovery beaches, not planted: plovers will not nest where they cannot see a predator coming.
records.role: A threatened beach-nesting plover that feeds on small invertebrates along the sand and the wrack line. Extremely sensitive to disturbance, it is a flagship indicator of protected, open dune beaches — and one of the few species here that is harmed rather than helped by planting.

requirements.hint: No water and no planting. Open bare sand, a roped-off closure so nobody walks through, and driftwood for the chicks to hide beside.

records.name: Black Turnstone
records.diet: Barnacles, limpets, small mussels, hermit crabs and other rocky-shore invertebrates
records.shelter: Rocky shoreline; tight flocks on raised rock at high tide
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky intertidal shores with barnacle and limpet crusts
records.fact: Turnstones flip over stones, shells and wrack to snatch the creatures hiding beneath — and hammer barnacles open with a short, wedge-shaped bill.
records.role: A rocky-shore forager that pries barnacles and limpets loose and flips wrack to find hidden prey. Like every shorebird it also needs somewhere safe to sit out high tide, when its feeding rocks are underwater — losing high-tide roosts costs a shore its turnstones even when the food is fine.

requirements.hint: Barnacle-crusted rock to feed on at low tide, and a raised roost to wait on when the tide covers it.

records.name: Anna's Hummingbird
records.diet: Flower nectar and small insects and spiders
records.shelter: A tiny cup of plant down and spider silk in a coastal shrub
records.preferredHabitat: Flowering coastal bluff and dune scrub
records.fact: Males climb about 30 m and dive, pulling up with a loud chirp made by their tail feathers, not their voice.
records.role: A year-round coastal hummingbird that feeds on nectar and small insects and pollinates the shrubs it feeds at. Winter-blooming manzanita is one of the few nectar sources available when Anna's is already nesting, which is why dune manzanita and not beachgrass is what brings it in — dune grasses are wind-pollinated and offer a hummingbird nothing.

requirements.hint: No water needed — it gets what it needs from nectar. Plant winter-flowering manzanita and salt-hardy scrub to nest in.

records.name: Ochre Sea Star
records.diet: Mussels above all, plus barnacles, limpets, chitons, snails and small urchins
records.shelter: Damp surge channels and rock crevices at the lower edge of the mussel bed
records.preferredHabitat: Wave-washed rocky intertidal with mussel beds above and surge below
records.fact: This is the animal the word 'keystone' was invented for — and since 2013 sea star wasting disease has killed ochre stars along thousands of kilometres of coast, and mussel beds have measurably spread down the rock in their place. Paine's experiment is being repeated by accident, at continental scale.
records.role: The textbook keystone predator of the rocky shore. By working upward from the low zone and eating mussels it sets the mussel bed's lower limit, keeping space open on the rock for barnacles, algae, anemones and dozens of other species. Remove it and the mussels take everything.

requirements.hint: Build the mussel bed first. The sea star lives at its lower edge — and that edge exists because the sea star is there.

sources.name: MARINe (UC Santa Cruz) — Pisaster and sea star wasting disease

records.name: Giant Green Anemone
records.diet: Crabs, detached mussels and small fish stung by its tentacles
records.shelter: The walls and floors of surge-flushed pools, characteristically just below the mussel beds
records.preferredHabitat: Clear, sunlit, surge-fed pools in the low zone
records.fact: Its green glow comes from algae living inside its tissues that hand over sugars they make from sunlight — which is why this anemone needs a sunlit pool, not a shaded one.
records.role: A sit-and-wait carnivore that catches prey the surf knocks off the rocks above it, while also farming symbiotic algae for extra food. It sits below the mussel beds and lives on what falls out of them, recycling dislodged shellfish and crabs.

requirements.hint: A sunlit pool with surge running through it, set below a mussel bed — its food arrives from above.

sources.name: Monterey Bay Aquarium — Giant green anemone

records.name: Black Oystercatcher
records.diet: Mussels and limpets above all, plus chitons, whelks and crabs
records.shelter: A shallow scrape on rock just above the high-tide line, decorated with shell chips and pebbles
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky intertidal reefs with mussel beds and no tall vegetation
records.fact: Despite the name, black oystercatchers hardly ever eat oysters — mussels and limpets are the real diet, and the long red bill is a chisel for cutting a shellfish's muscle before the shell can slam shut.
records.role: A rocky-shore specialist that pries mussels and limpets off the rock, timing its feeding to the tides. It nests just above the reach of the waves, so it needs both a mussel bed and undisturbed bare rock above it — a sensitive indicator of intertidal health.

requirements.hint: Mussels to eat and a bare rock scrape just above the tide to nest in. An oyster bed is not what this bird needs.

records.name: California Brown Pelican
records.diet: Small schooling fish, especially northern anchovy
records.shelter: Nests only on undisturbed offshore islands; loafs on sandbars and rocks
records.preferredHabitat: Anchovy-rich nearshore water within reach of an island colony
records.fact: Brown pelicans plunge-dive from up to about 60 feet, twisting as they hit so the impact does not break their neck.
records.role: A plunge-diving anchovy specialist whose recovery after DDT is one of the great conservation successes. It nests only on offshore islands, never on the mainland beach, and its colonies fail outright in years when the anchovy schools do not arrive — so a nesting pelican is a direct statement about the forage fish offshore.

requirements.hint: An island the tide and the footpaths cannot reach, quiet sandbars to loaf on, and anchovies in the water offshore.

records.name: Pigeon Guillemot
records.diet: Small fish taken near the bottom, plus crabs, worms and molluscs
records.shelter: Crevices in bluffs and gaps between boulders above the water
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky nesting bluffs over clear water less than about 30 m deep
records.fact: Pigeon guillemots have bright coral-red feet and matching red mouth linings, which they flash at each other in courtship.
records.role: A diving seabird that swims down to inspect the rocky seafloor for fish and prises invertebrates out of crevices. It nests in bluff cracks and gaps under boulders and forages in the shallow water that kelp forests keep productive.

requirements.hint: A bluff with crevices to nest in and clear, fish-rich water below it to dive through.

records.name: Sea Otter
records.diet: Sea urchins above all, plus mussels, clams, crabs and sea stars
records.shelter: Rafts wrapped in living surface kelp canopy, in coves calm enough to groom in
records.preferredHabitat: Kelp forest and rocky shore with abundant shellfish and calm rafting water
records.fact: Sea otters have no blubber at all — only the densest fur of any animal — so they must spend hours a day grooming it, and they wrap up in living kelp so they do not drift away while they sleep.
records.role: The keystone species of this coast. By eating sea urchins it stops them mowing the kelp down to bare rock, so kelp forests and everything they shelter persist. Take the otter away and urchins multiply, the kelp goes, and the forest becomes an urchin barren. Its kelp is living canopy, not dead wrack on the beach.

requirements.hint: Living kelp forest to raft in, a calm cove to groom in, and urchins and shellfish to eat. Beach wrack is dead kelp — it is no use to an otter.

records.name: Harbor Seal
records.diet: Fish, especially anchovy and flatfish, plus squid, octopus and crustaceans
records.shelter: Undisturbed low-tide rocks and sandbars used as haul-outs for resting and pupping
records.preferredHabitat: Calm, clean water beside a haul-out nobody walks up to
records.fact: Harbor seals can sleep in the water as well as on shore, hanging upright just below the surface.
records.role: A generalist marine predator that eats whatever fish is abundant and easy to catch. Its whole life ashore happens on haul-outs: seals rest, moult and give birth there, and a haul-out that people approach is a haul-out seals abandon. On this restored coast it sits at the top of the food web.

requirements.hint: Deep water to fish in and quiet rocks to haul out on. A seal haul-out is not a bird nesting closure — build the right one.

records.name: Creosote Bush
records.diet: Makes its own food from sunlight, air and water; takes nitrogen and minerals from the soil beneath it
records.shelter: Roots itself in open, uncompacted desert soil, spaced far from its neighbours
records.preferredHabitat: Open desert flats and lower slopes with deep, undisturbed soil
records.fact: Creosote bushes clone themselves outward in slowly widening rings, and the oldest known ring in the Mojave has been alive for thousands of years.
records.role: The dominant shrub of the Sonoran and Mojave deserts and the base of this biome's food web. Its resin-coated leaves lose almost no water, its flowers and buds feed desert iguanas and chuckwallas, its shade shelters rodents and lizards, and its dead leaves and stems are the litter that termites and darkling beetles return to the soil.

requirements.hint: Creosote needs living soil, not water: a crust to hold the ground together and termite-worked earth that rain can soak into.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service FEIS — Larrea tridentata

records.name: Saguaro
records.diet: Makes its own food from sunlight; stores months of rainwater in its pleated, expanding stem
records.shelter: Starts life in the shade of a nurse tree such as palo verde or ironwood, which shields the seedling from sun and frost
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky bajada slopes and well-drained ground in the Sonoran Desert
records.fact: A saguaro takes about 35 years to flower for the first time and may be 75 years old before it grows a single arm.
records.role: The Sonoran Desert's keystone plant. Its night-opening flowers feed bats, doves and bees; its June fruit is the richest food of the pre-monsoon desert; and the cavities woodpeckers carve in its trunk become nest sites for elf owls, kestrels and pygmy-owls for decades afterwards. It cannot establish without a nurse tree.

requirements.hint: No saguaro grows in the open. Plant a nurse tree first — the seedling spends its first decades in that shade.

sources.name: NPS — Saguaro National Park: Saguaro Cactus

records.name: Desert Subterranean Termite
records.diet: Dead grass, fallen leaves, dry dung and the weathered outer surfaces of dead wood
records.shelter: Tunnels and chambers underground, plus mud sheeting built over the litter it is eating
records.preferredHabitat: Soil beneath shrubs and grasses where dead plant litter collects
records.fact: These termites plaster a thin mud crust over dead stems and eat underneath it, so they can feed in full desert sun without ever touching dry air.
records.role: The desert's principal decomposer. In hot deserts there are too few fungi and too little moisture for litter to rot the way it does in a forest, so subterranean termites process most of the dead plant material instead — returning nitrogen and carbon to the soil and opening tunnels that let rain soak in rather than run off. When they swarm, nearly every insect-eater in the biome feeds on them.

requirements.hint: Work dead stems down into the soil. Subterranean termites never cross open ground — they reach their food from below.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service — Physical and chemical alteration of soil by two subterranean termite species in a Sonoran desert grassland

records.name: Pinacate Beetle
records.diet: Fallen leaves, dead stems, seeds and other dry plant litter on the soil surface
records.shelter: Under litter, stones and shrub bases by day; wanders in the open at dusk
records.preferredHabitat: Shrub-litter mounds and open ground between desert shrubs
records.fact: Threatened, a pinacate beetle stands on its head and points its rear end at you — and if you keep coming, it sprays a dark, foul-smelling chemical.
records.role: The desert's conspicuous surface detritivore. It shreds fallen leaves, stems and seeds into fragments that soil microbes and termites can finish, and its slow, flightless wandering makes it steady food for scorpions, burrowing owls, roadrunners and antelope squirrels — one of the few animals that will risk the spray.

requirements.hint: Let the leaf litter pile up under the shrubs. That drift is both the beetle's food and its daytime hiding place.

sources.name: Sky Island Alliance — Creature Feature: Pinacate Beetles

records.name: Black-tailed Jackrabbit
records.diet: Grasses, forbs, cactus, and the twigs and bark of desert shrubs
records.shelter: Shade forms scraped under shrubs; it never digs a burrow
records.preferredHabitat: Open flats with scattered shrubs and running room
records.fact: A jackrabbit's enormous ears are radiators — it lies still in the shade and dumps body heat into the air through the blood vessels in them.
records.role: The biome's largest common herbivore and the main prey package for its predators. Born fully furred and open-eyed in a surface scrape, it relies on speed and cover rather than a burrow. Coyotes, kit foxes and ravens all take jackrabbits, and a fallen one feeds the desert's scavengers.

requirements.hint: Grass to graze, shrubs to browse, and a shaded scrape to lie in. It gets its water from the plants — no drinking source needed.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service FEIS — Lepus californicus

records.name: Merriam's Kangaroo Rat
records.diet: Seeds, carried in fur-lined cheek pouches and cached underground
records.shelter: Shallow burrows under shrubs, plugged with sand every dawn
records.preferredHabitat: Loose soil beneath seed-bearing shrubs and mesquite
records.fact: Kangaroo rats never sweat or pant, and make all the water they need out of the dry seeds they eat.
records.role: A seed-eating rodent that shapes which plants come up, because the seeds it buries and forgets are the ones that germinate. Its burrows are the starting point for other diggers — kit foxes widen them into dens, and desert iguanas shelter in the ones dug at the base of creosote bushes. It feeds nearly every predator in the biome.

requirements.hint: Seed plants and diggable soil. Build no water — this animal may go its whole life without a drink.

records.name: Sonoran Desert Tortoise
records.diet: Native grasses, annual wildflowers, and cactus pads and fruit
records.shelter: Caliche caves, rock crevices and burrows under boulders on rocky slopes
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky bajada slopes with native grasses and wildflowers
records.fact: A Sonoran desert tortoise can live 80 years and spends about 95% of its life sheltering — usually in a caliche cave or rock den rather than a burrow it dug itself.
records.role: A long-lived herbivore and ecosystem engineer. The dens it digs out and enlarges are used long afterwards by burrowing owls, snakes, lizards, rodents and insects, so protecting one tortoise protects a whole set of animals that never dig for themselves. Adults are nearly predator-free; ravens and coyotes take hatchlings and juveniles, whose shells stay soft for years.

requirements.hint: A caliche den on a rocky slope, with grass and wildflowers to graze. It drinks only when rain pools appear, and can go a year without.

sources.name: Desert Tortoise Council — Biology of Desert Tortoises

records.name: Desert Iguana
records.diet: Creosote bush leaves, buds and flowers, with some other desert plants
records.shelter: Rodent burrows at the base of creosote bushes
records.preferredHabitat: Hot sandy flats where creosote is the dominant shrub
records.fact: Desert iguanas stay out feeding at around 40 degrees Celsius, in heat that has driven every other lizard underground.
records.role: A heat-loving herbivorous lizard tied almost entirely to one plant: it climbs into creosote bushes to eat their leaves and flowers and shelters in the rodent burrows dug into the soil mounds at their bases. Where creosote is grazed or cleared away, the iguana goes with it. Rattlesnakes and kit foxes hunt it.

requirements.hint: Creosote to eat and a burrowed creosote mound to escape into. It takes all its water from the leaves.

records.name: Common Chuckwalla
records.diet: Annual wildflowers, creosote and brittlebush leaves, buds and fruit
records.shelter: Rock crevices among boulders
records.preferredHabitat: Boulder piles with wildflowers and shrubs to graze nearby
records.fact: A threatened chuckwalla wedges into a crack and gulps air to inflate its lungs, locking itself in so tightly that a predator cannot pull it out.
records.role: A large plant-eating lizard that grazes annual wildflowers, creosote and brittlebush and basks on warm stone between meals. Its lung-inflation trick defeats snakes entirely, so its real predators are the ones that can dig or wait it out — coyotes above all.

requirements.hint: Deep crevices to wedge into, sun-warmed stone to bask on, and wildflowers and shrubs to graze. No water needed.

records.name: Cactus Bee
records.diet: Pollen and nectar from prickly pear and cholla flowers
records.shelter: Vertical nest burrows dug in bare, uncompacted ground, often with a small mud chimney at the entrance
records.preferredHabitat: Blooming prickly pear and cholla beside open, undisturbed soil
records.fact: Each female digs and stocks her own nest — but thousands of these single mothers dig side by side in the same patch of bare ground, so the ground hums.
records.role: The chief pollinator of prickly pear and cholla: no bee visits means no fruit set, and no fruit means no midsummer water for the animals that live on cactus fruit. It needs bare, loose, undisturbed soil to nest in, which is exactly what livestock trampling destroys — which makes it the clearest reason overgrazing matters here.

requirements.hint: Cactus flowers to work and a patch of soft, unpacked ground to nest in. Hard-trampled ground is unusable.

sources.name: Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum — Cactus Bee nesting sites

records.name: Costa's Hummingbird
records.diet: Nectar from chuparosa, ocotillo, creosote and desert lavender, plus small insects and spiders
records.shelter: Small cup nest of plant down and spider silk in a desert shrub or low tree
records.preferredHabitat: Desert washes and flats with winter- and spring-flowering shrubs
records.fact: A courting male dives past the female with a shrill whistle made by his tail feathers, flaring his violet throat like a moustache.
records.role: A desert hummingbird and pollinator that follows the bloom, arriving with the winter flowers of chuparosa and moving on as the desert dries. Because it feeds on nectar it does not need to drink, and it survives the hottest hours by dropping into torpor. Roadrunners and other quick predators catch it.

requirements.hint: Real flowers, not a feeder: chuparosa blooms right through the desert winter, and ocotillo takes over in spring.

sources.name: Sonoran Joint Venture — Costa's Hummingbird species account
Cornell Lab All About Birds — Costa's Hummingbird Life History

records.name: Gambel's Quail
records.diet: Seeds and green leaves, plus cactus fruit and, for the chicks, insects
records.shelter: Ground nests under shrubs; the covey roosts up in dense thorny cover at night
records.preferredHabitat: Thorny thickets along desert washes, within walking distance of water
records.fact: A male sentinel calls from a high perch while the rest of the covey feeds below, and the whole group runs rather than flies when he sounds the alarm.
records.role: A social ground bird that eats mostly seeds and greens but raises its chicks on insects, so it sits between the herbivores and the insect-eaters. Unlike most of this biome it genuinely needs to drink, and coveys walk to seeps and rock tanks daily through the summer. Coyotes take adults; ravens and roadrunners take eggs and chicks.

requirements.hint: Thorny thickets to roost in, seeds to eat — and unlike most desert animals here, water it can actually drink.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Gambel's Quail Life History

records.name: Gila Woodpecker
records.diet: Insects, saguaro fruit, mistletoe berries and other fruit
records.shelter: Cavities it excavates in living saguaros
records.preferredHabitat: Saguaro stands with mesquite and washes nearby
records.fact: It carves a hole in a living saguaro and then waits months for the cactus to seal the walls with hard scar tissue before it will nest inside.
records.role: The desert's keystone builder. It is the only animal here that can make a cavity, and its old holes go on to house elf owls, pygmy-owls, kestrels, flycatchers and native bees for years. It is also a heavy saguaro fruit eater and so a saguaro seed disperser — it depends on the plant and the plant depends on it. Rattlesnakes take it at the nest.

requirements.hint: Saguaros to carve into and saguaro fruit to eat. Prickly pear pads cannot hold a nest cavity — only a tall columnar cactus can.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Gila Woodpecker Life History

records.name: Phainopepla
records.diet: Desert mistletoe berries in winter, flying insects the rest of the year
records.shelter: Small cup nest in a mesquite or ironwood, usually in a clump of mistletoe
records.preferredHabitat: Mesquite stands carrying desert mistletoe, with water nearby
records.fact: A phainopepla can eat over a thousand mistletoe berries in a day, and the seeds pass through it still sticky, so it glues the next generation of mistletoe onto branches as it goes.
records.role: Desert mistletoe's key seed disperser, and almost the only animal that will eat the berries. The plant grows only on mesquite, ironwood, palo verde and acacia, so the bird needs those trees as much as the mistletoe does. It switches to catching insects on the wing outside the berry season. Roadrunners and snakes take it.

requirements.hint: Mistletoe on a mesquite is the whole story — the berries are the food and the clump is the nest site. Berries are watery, but it still drinks.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Phainopepla Life History

records.name: Harris's Antelope Squirrel
records.diet: Cactus fruit and seeds, green shoots, and insects
records.shelter: Burrows and cracks under rocks and cactus
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky desert with cactus in fruit
records.fact: It runs with its tail arched flat over its back like a parasol, then flattens itself belly-down on shaded ground to dump the heat it picked up.
records.role: A daytime omnivore that stays active in midday heat when almost everything else has gone underground. It has no way to make its own water, so it depends on succulent cactus fruit — which only sets where cactus bees have pollinated the flowers. Coyotes, kit foxes, roadrunners and rattlesnakes hunt it.

requirements.hint: It cannot survive on dry seeds alone — it needs juicy cactus fruit, and that means the bees have to come first.

records.name: Cactus Wren
records.diet: Insects and spiders, with some cactus fruit and seeds
records.shelter: Football-shaped grass nests built deep inside cholla
records.preferredHabitat: Desert with dense cholla and scattered trees
records.fact: Cactus wrens build several football-shaped nests and use the spares as bedrooms all year, sleeping surrounded by cholla spines.
records.role: The largest wren in North America, gleaning insects and spiders off the ground and out of shrubs and getting nearly all its water from that food. Its nest is built inside a cholla, where the spines keep snakes and most birds out — take the cholla away and the wren has nowhere to breed. Snakes and roadrunners still reach some nests.

requirements.hint: Cholla is the nest — nothing else in the desert is spiny enough. It takes all its water from insects and fruit.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Cactus Wren Life History

records.name: Burrowing Owl
records.diet: Large insects — beetles, termites, grasshoppers and crickets — plus small rodents and scorpions
records.shelter: Underground burrows dug by other animals; it cannot dig its own
records.preferredHabitat: Open ground with short, sparse vegetation and ready-made burrows
records.fact: Cornered in its burrow it makes a dry rasping hiss, and scientists think it may be copying a rattlesnake to scare intruders off.
records.role: A small ground owl that hunts insects by day and rodents at night, and one of the clearest examples in the biome of an animal that cannot make its own home. Every pair depends on a burrow something else dug — a tortoise, a ground squirrel or a badger — so its numbers rise and fall with the diggers. Coyotes are its main predator.

requirements.hint: It cannot dig. Bring the tortoise back first, then its old den becomes the owl's nest — with low, open ground to hunt over.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Burrowing Owl Life History

records.name: Regal Horned Lizard
records.diet: Harvester ants, which make up roughly 88% of what it eats, plus termites and a few other insects
records.shelter: Buries itself in loose sand; shelters under low shrubs
records.preferredHabitat: Open, sandy bare ground between shrubs, near harvester ant mounds
records.fact: A cornered horned lizard can squeeze blood out of the corners of its eyes in a jet that carries a metre or more — and it is aimed at foxes and coyotes, which find the taste foul.
records.role: An ant specialist so committed that its stomach is huge for its body, because harvester ants are low-value food and it must eat hundreds a day. It needs the open bare ground between shrubs where harvester ants make their cleared mounds, which is why it disappears from tidy, planted or heavily disturbed desert. Roadrunners, coyotes and ravens take it.

requirements.hint: No ants, no horned lizard. Harvester ants need open bare ground, not rock piles — leave the gaps between shrubs clear.

records.name: Common Raven
records.diet: Carrion above all, plus eggs, nestlings, young reptiles, insects and cactus fruit
records.shelter: Bulky stick nests on cliffs, in saguaros and ironwoods — and, increasingly, on power poles and billboards
records.preferredHabitat: Open desert with tall nest structures and a reliable food supply
records.fact: Ravens remember individual human faces and hold grudges, and a pair will work together to distract an animal while the other steals its food.
records.role: The desert's scavenger and cleanup crew: it finds carcasses first and starts the process that returns them to the soil. It is also the best human-impact story here. Roads, landfills, farms and power poles hand ravens free food, water and nest sites, so their numbers have risen far above what the desert alone would support — and those extra ravens kill juvenile desert tortoises, whose shells stay soft for years. Reducing raven subsidies is now central to tortoise recovery.

requirements.hint: Ravens follow food and water. A carcass left where it fell, a tall nest site, and something to drink — that is all they ask, which is exactly the problem.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Common Raven Life History
USFWS — Environmental Assessment to Reduce Common Raven Predation on the Desert Tortoise

records.name: Greater Roadrunner
records.diet: Lizards, large insects, scorpions, small birds, rodents and snakes
records.shelter: A bulky stick nest a metre or two up in a thorny shrub or cholla
records.preferredHabitat: Open running ground broken up by thorny thickets
records.fact: It runs down its prey at over 30 km/h and beats large or dangerous animals against a rock before swallowing them head-first.
records.role: The desert's chief daytime hunter of reptiles and large arthropods, and one of very few birds that will attack a rattlesnake. It needs both halves of its habitat: open ground to sprint across and a thorny thicket to nest in, safe from coyotes. Coyotes are its own main predator.

requirements.hint: Open ground to run on and a thorn thicket to nest in — plus lizards and big insects to chase down.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Greater Roadrunner Life History

records.name: Western Diamondback Rattlesnake
records.diet: Rodents and small mammals, with birds and lizards taken occasionally
records.shelter: Rock crevices and burrows; deep frost-free fissures in winter
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky shelter within reach of busy rodent runways
records.fact: It adds a rattle segment every time it sheds, but segments break off, so counting them tells you nothing about its age.
records.role: An ambush predator that waits on rodent trails, strikes, releases, and follows the scent trail to its meal. It swallows prey whole and may eat only once every few weeks, which makes it a slow but persistent control on rodent numbers. Roadrunners and coyotes kill it; in winter it returns to the same rock den year after year.

requirements.hint: A deep winter den it can return to every year, warm rock to ambush from, and rodents on the move.

sources.name: Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum — Western Diamondback Rattlesnake

records.name: Giant Desert Hairy Scorpion
records.diet: Beetles, termites, crickets, spiders, centipedes and other scorpions
records.shelter: A spiral burrow it digs itself, up to about two and a half metres deep
records.preferredHabitat: Loose diggable soil with litter and stone cover to hunt over at night
records.fact: Scorpions glow blue-green under ultraviolet light, and nobody is entirely sure why.
records.role: The largest scorpion in North America and the top arthropod predator of the night shift, taking beetles, termites, spiders and even other scorpions. Its deep burrow, not the rocks on the surface, is what really keeps it alive: it spends most of the year down there escaping heat and dryness. Elf owls, burrowing owls and roadrunners hunt it.

requirements.hint: Rocks are only the day cover — what it really needs is soil deep and loose enough to dig metres down into.

records.name: Elf Owl
records.diet: Moths, beetles, crickets and scorpions
records.shelter: Old woodpecker cavities in saguaros and desert trees; it cannot excavate its own
records.preferredHabitat: Saguaro stands and mesquite washes with woodpecker holes
records.fact: The world's lightest owl weighs about as much as a golf ball, and it nips the stinger off a scorpion before carrying it home to the chicks.
records.role: A migratory night hunter of insects and scorpions, and a textbook secondary cavity nester: it cannot make a hole, so every nest it uses was carved by a Gila woodpecker and then hardened by the saguaro into a waterproof 'boot'. No woodpeckers means no elf owls, however many saguaros are standing.

requirements.hint: Saguaros alone are not enough — a Gila woodpecker has to carve the hole first. Then the cactus seals it into a boot the owl can nest in.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Elf Owl Life History

records.name: Kit Fox
records.diet: Kangaroo rats and other rodents, jackrabbits, lizards, insects and some fruit
records.shelter: Cool underground dens with several entrances, usually rodent burrows it has widened
records.preferredHabitat: Open desert with loose soil and abundant small prey
records.fact: The smallest wild dog in North America, its oversized ears both pick up rodents moving in the dark and shed body heat like radiators.
records.role: A small nocturnal desert fox that lives almost entirely on rodents and rarely needs to drink, taking its water from prey. It seldom digs a den from scratch — it takes over and enlarges a kangaroo rat or ground squirrel burrow, so it needs a rodent population before it needs anything else. Several entrances give it escape routes from coyotes, which are its main threat.

requirements.hint: Rodents first — the fox's den is a kangaroo rat burrow made bigger. It takes its water from what it eats.

sources.name: USFWS — San Joaquin Kit Fox (Vulpes macrotis mutica)

records.name: Coyote
records.diet: Rabbits, rodents, birds, reptiles, carrion, cactus fruit and mesquite pods
records.shelter: Earthen dens dug into the cut banks of dry washes
records.preferredHabitat: Open desert with washes, cover and plenty of prey
records.fact: A howling pair sounds like a whole pack — each coyote shifts pitch as it calls, an illusion biologists call the beau geste effect.
records.role: The top predator of this desert and the most adaptable mammal in it, hunting rabbits and rodents but also eating fruit, pods and carrion when they are easier. It is the only animal here that regularly kills kit foxes, roadrunners and burrowing owls, and it digs its den into the bank of a wash rather than out on the open flat.

requirements.hint: A den dug into a wash bank above the flood line, cover to hunt from, prey on the move — and unlike most animals here, it drinks.

records.name: White Oak
records.diet: Makes its own sugar from sunlight, water and air. Water and minerals come in through a partnership with fungi wrapped around its root tips.
records.shelter: Needs none, and gives a great deal: bark crevices, dead limbs, heart-rot cavities and a canopy full of caterpillars.
records.preferredHabitat: Well-drained upland slopes and ridges in eastern deciduous forest; a seedling needs light reaching the forest floor, which is why oaks come back after a gap opens.
records.fact: Oaks feed more kinds of caterpillar than any other North American tree — several hundred species on a single genus — which is why so many songbirds nest where the oaks are.
records.role: The white oak is this forest's primary producer and its mast tree. Every acorn eater in the biome is ultimately living on sunlight the oak captured, and in a good mast year one tree can drop thousands of acorns. Its leaves feed the caterpillar layer that forest birds raise their chicks on, its roots trade sugar to fungi for soil nutrients, and its dead limbs become the cavities half the roster nests in. Oaks regenerate slowly and deer eat the seedlings, so a logged-over woodland does not get its oaks back on its own.

requirements.hint: Acorns, light reaching the ground, and a fence — deer eat oak seedlings faster than oaks can grow. No pond needed: white oak holds the dry ridges.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service FEIS — Quercus alba
National Wildlife Federation — Keystone native plants

records.name: Eastern Hemlock
records.diet: Photosynthesis — and unusually little of it, because hemlock is built to grow slowly in deep shade rather than fast in the open.
records.shelter: Provides winter shelter rather than needing it: the dense evergreen crown holds snow off the ground beneath it.
records.preferredHabitat: Cool, damp, shaded slopes, ravines and streamsides; seedlings establish best on rotting logs and moss rather than bare leaf litter.
records.fact: Hemlock casts the deepest shade of any eastern tree, and the ground and water beneath a hemlock stand stay measurably cooler through summer than the forest around it.
records.role: Eastern hemlock is a foundation species: it does not just live in the forest, it sets the conditions other species live in. Its shade keeps streams cold, its canopy makes snow-free ground that deer and other animals use in winter, and its inner bark carries porcupines through the season when nothing green is left. It partners with underground fungi for nutrients. Hemlock takes centuries to replace and is now being killed across its range by the introduced hemlock woolly adelgid.

requirements.hint: Cool damp shade and a rotting log to germinate on — hemlock seeds that land on bare duff usually fail, and the ones that land on rotten wood become trees.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service FEIS — Tsuga canadensis

records.name: Turkey Tail
records.diet: Dead hardwood. It secretes enzymes into fallen logs, stumps and dead branches and absorbs what dissolves.
records.shelter: Lives as a web of threads inside the wood itself; only the banded fan-shaped brackets show on the outside.
records.preferredHabitat: Damp, shaded dead hardwood — fallen logs, stumps, dead limbs on living trees — anywhere wood is left where it falls.
records.fact: Lignin, the substance that makes wood woody, is so tough that almost nothing alive can digest it. White-rot fungi like turkey tail are among the few that can — without them a forest would slowly bury itself in its own dead wood.
records.role: Turkey tail is the forest's recycling system. It breaks dead wood back down into nutrients other plants can use, and while it does so it softens standing trunks until a woodpecker can chisel into them, hollows fallen logs into salamander nurseries and small-mammal dens, and turns solid trunks into the punky wood carpenter ants colonise. Almost every cavity in this biome starts as a fungus. Clearing away deadwood removes the whole process.

requirements.hint: Dead hardwood left where it fell, and enough shade to keep it damp. No open water required — the fungus lives on the moisture held inside the log.

sources.name: Macalester College Ordway Natural History Study Area — Turkey Tail Fungus

records.name: Deer Truffle
records.diet: Sugar traded from living oak and hemlock roots, plus nitrogen and phosphorus it pulls out of the leaf litter and passes back to the trees.
records.shelter: Underground. It sheathes living tree root tips and fruits as marble-sized tubers a few centimetres below the surface.
records.preferredHabitat: Deep, undisturbed duff and soil under mature oak, hemlock and pine — ground that has not been raked, scraped or compacted.
records.fact: A deer truffle never opens. It cannot release its spores into the air, so it smells strongly instead and waits to be dug up and eaten — flying squirrel droppings are full of its spores, which is how it reaches the next stand of trees.
records.role: This is a mycorrhizal fungus: a partner, not a parasite. Its threads extend a tree's root system many times over, mining nutrients out of the litter and trading them for sugar. Most forest trees depend on partnerships like this to grow at all. It also sits near the bottom of the food web as food — flying squirrels and chipmunks dig it up, and the spores that survive the trip plant the fungus somewhere new. A forest floor stripped to bare soil loses the network first and the trees second.
eatsOther: sugars from oak and hemlock roots

requirements.hint: Living oak and hemlock roots to partner with, and deep undisturbed duff to grow through. Raked or compacted ground has no fungal network left in it.

sources.name: USGS — Hypogeous sequestrate fungi (Elaphomyces) at small-mammal foraging sites
First Nature — Elaphomyces granulatus, False Truffle
USDA Forest Service — Northern flying squirrel (Glaucomys sabrinus) ecology

records.name: Polyphemus Moth
records.diet: As a caterpillar, tree leaves — oak, birch, hickory, maple, willow. The adult moth has no working mouth and never eats anything at all.
records.shelter: Spins a tough silk cocoon wrapped in a leaf; the cocoon falls with the leaves in autumn and overwinters on the forest floor.
records.preferredHabitat: Broadleaf woodland and woodland edge with oak, birch and hickory, and an undisturbed litter layer beneath them.
records.fact: The adult moth has no working mouthparts. Everything it will ever spend — finding a mate, laying eggs, the whole last week of its life — was eaten by the caterpillar.
records.role: This moth stands for the caterpillar layer, the step almost every forest bird depends on and the one this biome was missing entirely. Caterpillars turn tough tree leaves into soft protein, and it is caterpillars, not seeds, that nearly all woodland songbirds feed their chicks. Adults feed the bats that hunt at dusk. Because the cocoons spend winter in fallen leaves, a woodland raked bare in autumn loses next year's moths along with the leaves.

requirements.hint: Broadleaf host trees for the caterpillars and leaf litter left alone over winter for the cocoons.

sources.name: Butterflies and Moths of North America — Antheraea polyphemus

records.name: Wood Duck
records.diet: Acorns, seeds and aquatic plants; ducklings eat insects and snails for their first weeks
records.shelter: Obligate cavity nester — old woodpecker holes and natural hollows in trees over or beside water
records.preferredHabitat: Wooded ponds, sloughs and slow backwaters with big cavity trees standing in or near the water
records.fact: A day after hatching, wood duck ducklings jump from nest cavities up to 50 feet above the ground and bounce unhurt.
records.role: The wood duck is the clearest secondary cavity user in this forest: it cannot make a hole and cannot nest without one, so its return depends entirely on the woodpeckers arriving first. It moves acorns and aquatic plant seeds between the forest and the water, and it feeds owls, raccoons and foxes. Wood ducks nearly vanished a century ago, and cavity supply is still what limits them.

requirements.hint: An old woodpecker hole in a snag standing over quiet water, with oaks nearby for acorns. No woodpecker, no wood duck.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Wood Duck life history

records.name: Northern Flying Squirrel
records.diet: Mostly underground truffle fungi; also lichens, acorns, tree seeds and some insects
records.shelter: Old woodpecker cavities and natural hollows; huddles in groups through winter to stay warm
records.preferredHabitat: Cool, closed-canopy hemlock and northern-hardwood forest with old cavity trees and a deep fungal layer in the soil
