records.fact: Fungal spores turn up in nearly every flying squirrel dropping, which makes this squirrel one of the main ways underground truffle fungi get from one stand of trees to the next.
records.role: The flying squirrel is a fungivore — a primary consumer that lives on fungi rather than plants — and a keystone mutualist. It digs up truffles, and the spores that survive the trip inoculate new tree roots, so the squirrel, the fungus and the trees are one loop. It is also a secondary cavity user that cannot excavate, and a favourite prey of owls and fishers, which means it carries energy from the fungal layer straight to the top of the web.

requirements.hint: Truffles in the soil to eat and an old woodpecker cavity to sleep in — this squirrel makes neither for itself.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service — Northern flying squirrel ecology and diet

records.name: Pileated Woodpecker
records.diet: Carpenter ants and wood-boring beetle larvae above all; also berries and nuts
records.shelter: Excavates a new rectangular nest cavity each year in a large dead snag, and leaves last year's behind
records.preferredHabitat: Mature forest with large-diameter standing snags and plenty of big fallen logs on the ground
records.fact: Its deep rectangular excavations can be large enough to snap a small tree in half.
records.role: This is the keystone species of the forest. It cuts a new nest cavity every spring and abandons it, and those holes become the nest and den sites of wood ducks, flying squirrels, fishers, bats and owls — animals that cannot make holes of their own. It needs two things a logged forest lacks: snags big enough to hold a cavity, and fallen logs rotted enough for carpenter ants. Restore those and a dozen other species follow it in.

requirements.hint: Big snags — plural, and large-diameter — plus rotted logs on the ground full of carpenter ants.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Pileated Woodpecker life history

records.name: Little Brown Bat
records.diet: Strict insectivore: midges, caddisflies, mayflies, moths and mosquitoes, most of them hatched out of water
records.shelter: Day-roosts under loose slabs of bark and in tree cavities and buildings; hibernates in caves and mines
records.preferredHabitat: Forest with open water — ponds, pools and slow streams — to hunt over at dusk
records.fact: White-nose syndrome, a cold-loving fungus that wakes bats during hibernation until they burn through their fat, has killed more than 90% of little brown bats at many hibernation sites.
records.role: A little brown bat can eat close to half its own body weight in insects in a night, which makes it the biome's main check on the night-flying insect layer. Nearly everything it eats begins life as a larva in water, so it links the pond to the forest: no water, no insects, no bats. It roosts under bark that only comes loose on dead and dying trees, and it feeds owls and nest-raiding raccoons.

requirements.hint: Loose bark to sleep under by day and open water to hunt over at dusk — almost everything a little brown bat eats hatches out of a pond.

sources.name: US Fish & Wildlife Service — Little Brown Bat

records.name: Barred Owl
records.diet: Small mammals above all — squirrels, chipmunks, mice, voles — plus birds, amphibians, crayfish and fish
records.shelter: A natural cavity 20–40 ft up in a large tree, usually a broken-topped trunk hollowed by heart rot; sometimes an old stick nest
records.preferredHabitat: Large blocks of mature forest, very often near water
records.fact: Barred owls sometimes wade into shallow water to catch fish and crayfish — unusual hunting for a woodland owl.
records.role: The barred owl is the night-hunting mid-level predator of mature forest, taking squirrels, chipmunks, amphibians and, at the water's edge, crayfish. It is a secondary cavity user like the nuthatch and the wood duck, but it needs a hole far bigger than any woodpecker cuts, so it has to wait for a tree old enough to have rotted hollow — which is why it is an indicator of forest age. Its own predator is the great horned owl.

requirements.hint: A hollow chimney in a big old tree, mature forest around it, and shallow water to wade for crayfish.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Barred Owl life history

records.name: Fisher
records.diet: Small and medium mammals — porcupines, squirrels, hares — plus birds, carrion and fruit
records.shelter: Dens in hollow logs and ground burrows; kits are raised in a cavity high inside a living tree
records.preferredHabitat: Unbroken conifer and mixed forest with a closed canopy and large hollow trees
records.fact: The fisher is one of very few predators that regularly kills porcupines, circling to slash at the face until it can flip the porcupine over and reach the quill-free belly.
records.role: The fisher is a mid-level forest predator and the main check on porcupine numbers, which otherwise damage a lot of timber. It hunts in the trees as readily as on the ground and takes squirrels and flying squirrels other predators miss. Because it needs continuous canopy and big hollow trees for its natal dens, a fisher's presence is a reliable sign that the forest is mature and connected rather than fragmented.

requirements.hint: Closed canopy, a big living tree hollow enough to raise kits high off the ground, and porcupines below.

records.name: Showy Milkweed
records.diet: Makes its own sugars from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide; pulls minerals up through deep spreading rhizomes
records.shelter: Dies back each autumn and overwinters as a woody rootstock and rhizome network below the frost line
records.preferredHabitat: Sunny meadow swales, streambanks and roadsides with deep soil that stays damp into early summer
records.fact: Milkweed sap is loaded with bitter, heart-stopping cardenolides — monarch caterpillars eat it anyway and store the poison in their own bodies.
records.role: A primary producer and the base of this meadow's food chain. It is the only kind of plant a monarch caterpillar can grow up on, its wide flower umbels feed bumble bees and leafcutter bees through midsummer, and the aphid colonies on its stems are what lady beetles hunt. Milkweed spreads by underground rhizomes, so one planting slowly becomes a patch.

requirements.hint: Break open a damp low swale, sow it, and keep native grass around it — showy milkweed needs bare soil to start and moisture through its first summer.

sources.name: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Showy Milkweed
Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center — Asclepias speciosa

records.name: Blue Grama
records.diet: Photosynthesises; a warm-season bunchgrass that stores food in its crown and fine root mat
records.shelter: Survives drought and grazing as a low tuft with growing points at ground level, protected from teeth and hooves
records.preferredHabitat: Open, sunny shortgrass prairie and dry meadow on well-drained soil
records.fact: Blue grama's seed heads curl over like tiny eyelashes, and its roots reach further down into the soil than the plant stands tall.
records.role: The meadow's dominant grass and its main primary producer. Almost every plant-eater here — grasshoppers, voles, cottontails, ground squirrels, deer — eats it directly, so the amount of blue grama sets how much animal life the meadow can carry. Its dead stems and roots build the thatch layer that meadow fungi recycle back into soil.

requirements.hint: Plug live sod into bare ground. Blue grama is wind-pollinated and needs no watering once rooted — its roots find their own water.

sources.name: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center — Bouteloua gracilis
USDA Forest Service FEIS — Bouteloua gracilis

records.name: Meadow Mushroom
records.diet: Releases enzymes into dead grass roots, stems and thatch, then absorbs the sugars and minerals that dissolve
records.shelter: Spends most of its life as a hidden underground web of threads (mycelium); only the caps appear above ground
records.preferredHabitat: Old, undisturbed meadow and lightly grazed pasture with a deep layer of dead grass litter
records.fact: The mushrooms you see are only the fruit. The fungus itself is a web of threads in the soil that spreads outward a little each year, which is why the caps often come up in a ring.
records.role: The meadow's decomposer. It breaks dead grass litter back down into minerals that living plants take up again, closing the loop between the soil and the grass. Nothing else in this meadow can take apart tough dead plant material, so without fungi the thatch just piles up and the nutrients stay locked in it.

requirements.hint: Leave the dead grass where it falls. Fungi need litter to feed on and damp ground to fruit — tidy meadows have no decomposers.

sources.name: First Nature — Agaricus campestris, Field Mushroom

records.name: Margined Burying Beetle
records.diet: Adults and larvae feed on the carcasses of mice, voles and small birds, and on the fly maggots competing for them
records.shelter: Buries a small carcass in loose soil and raises its brood in the chamber underneath it
records.preferredHabitat: Open prairie and meadow with soft, uncompacted soil; thought to have been a western grassland species originally
records.fact: Both parents stay underground with their young, guarding the buried carcass and feeding the grubs mouth to mouth — parental care is rare in insects.
records.role: A detritivore that recycles dead animals. A pair finds a carcass by smell within hours, buries it out of reach of flies, strips the fur or feathers off and coats it to slow decay, then raises their larvae on it. Without burying beetles the meadow's carrion feeds flies instead of returning to the soil.
eatsOther: carcasses of mice and small birds

requirements.hint: Loose, uncompacted soil deep enough to bury a mouse — and small mammals in the meadow to supply the carcasses.

records.name: Leafcutter Bee
records.diet: Adults eat nectar and pollen from many flowering plants
records.shelter: Nests in hollow stems and beetle holes, lining each cell with cut leaf pieces
records.preferredHabitat: Meadows and gardens with diverse flowers and hollow-stem nesting cavities
records.fact: Female leafcutter bees snip neat circles from leaves to build and seal their nest cells.
records.role: A solitary native bee that pollinates a wide range of meadow plants, carrying pollen dry on the underside of its abdomen rather than in pollen baskets. It is an obligate cavity nester: every female needs a hollow stem or old beetle tunnel to line with leaf discs and provision for the next generation. Adults are caught by ambush predators.

requirements.hint: Hollow stems to nest in, flowers to forage on, and soft-edged leaves she can cut discs from.

records.name: American Goldfinch
records.diet: Almost entirely seeds — thistle, sunflower, aster, and grass seeds
records.shelter: Tightly woven cup nest lashed 1–3 m up in a shrub or small tree, bound with spider silk and lined with thistle down
records.preferredHabitat: Weedy fields and open areas with native thistle, sunflower, and asters
records.fact: Goldfinches are strict vegetarians and nest late in summer so thistle down is ready to line their nests.
records.role: A specialist granivore that thrives on native thistle and sunflower seed, dispersing composite seeds across the meadow. It is one of the few songbirds that feeds its nestlings almost entirely on seed. Being small and abundant, it is prey for agile bird-hunting hawks.

requirements.hint: Let the sunflowers and native thistles stand and go to seed — the down is what the late nest is lined with.

sources.name: Cornell All About Birds — American Goldfinch
Xerces Society — Standing Up for Native Thistles

records.name: California Mantis
records.diet: Ambush predator eating live insects — bees, grasshoppers, butterflies and more
records.shelter: Perches motionless on plants; glues a foam egg case (ootheca) to a stiff standing stem for the winter
records.preferredHabitat: Meadows and flowery edges with standing vegetation to ambush from
records.fact: A praying mantis can swivel its head almost 180 degrees — unique among insects — for a wide field of view.
records.role: A native sit-and-wait ambush predator that seizes prey with spined forelegs in a strike faster than a blink. It is an indiscriminate generalist, not a pest-control specialist: it takes grasshoppers, but also bumble bees, leafcutter bees and monarch caterpillars, so it eats pests and pollinators alike. Birds and gartersnakes take it in turn.

requirements.hint: Leave stiff dead stems standing over winter — that is where next year's egg case is glued.

sources.name: NC State Extension — Challenging the conventional wisdom about praying mantids

records.name: Killdeer
records.diet: Invertebrates — earthworms, grasshoppers, beetles, and snails
records.shelter: Nests in a bare ground scrape lined with pebbles and shell bits
records.preferredHabitat: Open, flat ground with very short grass and scattered stones
records.fact: Killdeer fake a broken wing, dragging it as if injured to lure predators away from the nest.
records.role: A ground-foraging insectivore that races and halts across open meadow, snapping up worms and insects. As abundant, exposed ground-nesters they are important prey for meadow hunters, which take adults, chicks, and eggs alike.

requirements.hint: Very short grass, open bare ground and scattered pebbles — deep bunchgrass is the opposite of killdeer habitat.

records.name: Western Bluebird
records.diet: Mainly ground insects (caterpillars, beetles, grasshoppers); berries in winter
records.shelter: Grass-lined nest inside tree cavities, old woodpecker holes, or nest boxes
records.preferredHabitat: Grassy openings with scattered trees and low perches to drop from
records.fact: Bluebirds cannot make their own nest holes, so nest-box trails put up by volunteers are a large part of why they came back.
records.role: A secondary cavity-nesting insectivore that hunts from a low perch and drops onto insects in short grass, switching to berries in winter. It cannot excavate, so it depends entirely on holes something else made — and in a meadow with no woodpecker, on nest boxes. It competes fiercely for those holes and is hunted by bird-catching hawks.

requirements.hint: It cannot dig its own hole. Put up a nest box, keep the grass short enough to hunt in, and add berries for winter.

sources.name: Birds of the World — Western Bluebird

records.name: Cooper's Hawk
records.diet: Mainly medium and small birds; also chipmunks, mice, and squirrels
records.shelter: Builds a stick nest high in a tree, on a limb or in a crotch
records.preferredHabitat: Woodland edges and hedgerows with open country and scattered trees near meadows
records.fact: Cooper's Hawks thread through dense cover at high speed to ambush songbirds — a risky style that leaves many with healed chest-bone fractures.
records.role: A bird-hunting mesopredator that patrols meadow edges and hedgerows for songbirds. Its agile, low pursuit flight lets it pluck sparrows, finches and bluebirds out of cover, so it needs a dense wooded edge to hunt along rather than open grass. Great Horned Owls kill it in turn.

requirements.hint: A dense hedgerow to ambush along and a tall tree to nest in — once there are enough songbirds to hunt.

sources.name: Cornell All About Birds — Cooper's Hawk
American Ornithological Society — 65th Supplement to the Check-list

records.name: American Badger
records.diet: Digs out ground squirrels, gophers, voles, and mice; also insects and bumble bee nests
records.shelter: Digs its own large underground burrows; a powerful excavator
records.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and grasslands with deep, stone-free, diggable soil and a rodent colony to hunt
records.fact: Badgers sometimes team up with coyotes: the badger digs prey out below while the coyote catches those that bolt above ground.
records.role: A fossorial carnivore that hunts by digging burrowing rodents straight out of their tunnels, so it needs both deep uncompacted soil and a living rodent colony. Its abandoned burrows benefit other animals. Adult badgers have essentially no predators in this meadow.

requirements.hint: Deep stone-free soil it can dig through, wide grass above it, and a ground squirrel colony to hunt. Rock piles are what badger country isn't.

records.name: Great Horned Owl
records.diet: The most varied diet of any North American raptor — rabbits, voles, ground squirrels, skunks, snakes, and other hawks and owls
records.shelter: Never builds a nest; takes over an old hawk or crow stick nest, a tree cavity, or a cliff ledge
records.preferredHabitat: Scattered tall trees and wooded edges with open grassland to hunt over
records.fact: Great Horned Owls don't build nests. They move into stick nests that Red-tailed Hawks and crows built the year before, which is why they lay eggs so early — the nests are empty in winter.
records.role: The meadow's night-time apex predator, and the only animal here that regularly kills other predators: fox kits, Cooper's Hawks and even Red-tailed Hawks are all on its list. Its return puts a ceiling on the mesopredator layer, which is what an apex predator is for. Because it cannot build its own nest, it can only settle where a stick-nesting hawk has nested first.

requirements.hint: It cannot build a nest of its own — a Red-tailed Hawk has to nest here first and leave one behind. Owls get their water from their prey.

sources.name: Cornell All About Birds — Great Horned Owl

records.name: Broadleaf Cattail
records.diet: Makes its own food from sunlight, carbon dioxide and water, drawing nutrients up through its roots from the marsh mud.
records.shelter: Survives winter as thick, starchy rhizomes buried in saturated mud below the frost line.
records.preferredHabitat: Sunlit saturated mud and standing water up to about half a metre deep along the marsh edge.
records.fact: One brown cattail head can release over 200,000 seeds, but they sprout only on bare, wet, sunlit mud — which is why drawing a marsh down for one summer brings the cattails back.
records.role: The marsh's main primary producer and the base of both of its food chains. Cattails turn sunlight into stems, roots and — above all — the dead leaf litter that feeds the wetland's detrital food web, and they build the standing cover most marsh birds nest in.

requirements.hint: Expose a patch of bare, wet, sunlit mud at the water's edge. Cattail seed will not sprout in shade or in deep water.

sources.name: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Broad-leaved Cattail

records.name: Wild Celery
records.diet: Photosynthesises underwater, using whatever light reaches it through the water column.
records.shelter: Overwinters as buds and tubers buried in the sediment.
records.preferredHabitat: Slow, clear water half a metre to two metres deep over soft, settled sediment.
records.fact: Wild celery sends a female flower to the surface on a long coiled stalk; once it is pollinated the stalk springs back into a coil and pulls the ripening seeds underwater.
records.role: The marsh's submerged producer and a living water-clarity gauge. It can only grow where enough light gets through the water, so a wild celery bed is proof the water is running clear — and its leaves, tubers and the film of algae on them feed ducks, turtles, muskrats and crayfish.

requirements.hint: Settle the silt out first. Wild celery is a light-hungry underwater plant — murky water is the one thing it cannot survive.

sources.name: USGS — American wildcelery (Vallisneria americana): ecological considerations for restoration

records.name: Freshwater Scud
records.diet: Dead leaves and stems, the fungi and bacteria growing on them, and algal film scraped off plants.
records.shelter: Among submerged litter, plant stems and the loose top layer of sediment.
records.preferredHabitat: Shallow, well-oxygenated water with a deep drift of decaying plant litter.
records.fact: A scud shreds one dead cattail leaf into thousands of fragments — and it is really after the fungi and bacteria coating those fragments, not the leaf itself.
records.role: The wetland's shredder. Far more plant material dies and falls in a marsh than is ever eaten alive, and scuds are what turn that litter into food the rest of the food web can use. They are also the single most abundant food of young fish and salamander larvae.

requirements.hint: Let the dead cattail leaves pile up underwater. Scuds live in the litter, not the open water.

sources.name: Biological Invasions — Potential impact of invasive amphipods on leaf litter recycling in aquatic ecosystems

records.name: Virile Crayfish
records.diet: Decaying plants and carcasses, live aquatic plants, snails, insect larvae and scuds.
records.shelter: Burrows dug into saturated banks, and gaps beneath sunken logs and stones.
records.preferredHabitat: Slow, weedy water with woody cover and a bank soft enough to dig into.
records.fact: If a crayfish loses a claw in a fight it simply grows a new one, a little larger at each moult, until the replacement matches the original.
records.role: The marsh's recycler and its most-eaten large invertebrate. Crayfish shred dead plants, clean up carcasses and turn buried detritus back into living tissue — which is then eaten by the otter, mink, kingfisher, bittern, merganser, crane, snapping turtle and both herons.

requirements.hint: Soft bank to dig into, sunken wood to hide under, and plenty of rotting plant material to eat.

sources.name: Reviews in Fisheries Science — Redefining the role of crayfish in aquatic ecosystems
Oecologia — Effects of crayfish on leaf processing and invertebrate colonisation of leaves

records.name: Giant Floater
records.diet: Algae, bacteria and fine dead particles strained out of the water.
records.shelter: Burrowed upright in stable fine sediment with only its two siphons showing.
records.preferredHabitat: Slow, settled water over firm silt and fine sand.
records.fact: A freshwater mussel starts life as a larva that must clamp onto the gills of a passing fish and ride there for weeks before dropping off — no fish, no next generation of mussels.
records.role: The marsh's water filter. A mussel bed strains algae and fine particles out of the water all day and drops them to the bottom as food for scuds and crayfish. Because the larvae cannot survive without host fish, mussels only return once the fish have.

requirements.hint: Mussels need a settled bed that stays put for years — and they need fish, because their larvae ride on fish gills before they can settle.

sources.name: NC Wildlife — General Life History for Mussels

records.name: Northern Leopard Frog
records.diet: Insects, spiders and worms taken in wet meadows and along the water's edge
records.shelter: Shallow water in spring; damp grassy meadow through the summer
records.preferredHabitat: Lily-fringed shallows with wet meadow beside them
records.fact: A startled leopard frog escapes in unpredictable zig-zag leaps that often carry it away from the water into thick grass, where its spots break up its outline.
records.role: A marsh frog that spends the summer hunting invertebrates in wet meadow well away from open water — which is why a wetland with no grassy margin loses its leopard frogs. It is key prey for both herons, the bittern and mink.

requirements.hint: A lily pool to breed in and a wide band of damp meadow beside it to spend the summer hunting in.

sources.name: National Park Service — Northern Leopard Frog

records.name: Marsh Wren
records.diet: Insects and spiders picked from marsh stems
records.shelter: Woven dome nests lashed among cattails and bulrushes
records.preferredHabitat: Cattail and bulrush stands over water
records.fact: A male marsh wren builds up to a dozen dummy nests for one female to choose from — and he will puncture the eggs of blackbirds and other wrens nesting nearby.
records.role: A tiny, feisty insectivore of the reeds. It gleans insects and spiders from stems, builds decoy nests to court a mate, and is one of the few songbirds that is itself a nest predator.

requirements.hint: Bulrush and cattail standing in water — the stiff stems a wren can weave a hanging ball nest between.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Marsh Wren life history

records.name: Snapping Turtle
records.diet: Carrion, fish, crayfish, aquatic plants and almost anything else it can catch
records.shelter: Muddy pond bottoms; females travel overland to sandy banks to nest
records.preferredHabitat: Deep still water with a soft mud bottom and a sandy rise to nest on
records.fact: Adult snapping turtles have almost no natural predators and can live for decades — but their eggs and hatchlings are eaten by almost everything, so a single nest bank matters more than any adult.
records.role: A heavily armoured scavenger and omnivore lurking on the pond bottom. It cleans up carcasses, takes fish, crayfish and ducklings, and grazes plants — the marsh's clean-up crew as much as its predator.

requirements.hint: Deep still water with a soft bottom, plus a warm sandy rise above the waterline for the females to dig their nests in.

records.name: American Bittern
records.diet: Fish, frogs, insects and crayfish
records.shelter: Platform nests bent down from living reeds, hidden low over shallow water
records.preferredHabitat: Tall marsh vegetation standing in shallow water
records.fact: The bittern freezes bill-skyward and sways with the wind, so its streaked throat lines up with the reeds and it simply disappears.
records.role: A secretive ambush predator of the reed beds. It stands motionless, then seizes fish, frogs and crayfish, relying entirely on camouflage — which means it needs its reeds unbroken and deep, not just present.

requirements.hint: Reeds thick enough to vanish in, standing in shallow water, with a low hidden nest platform bent down among the stems.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — American Bittern life history

records.name: Belted Kingfisher
records.diet: Small fish and crayfish
records.shelter: Tunnel burrows dug a metre or more into bare earthen banks
records.preferredHabitat: Clear water with a bare vertical bank beside it and perches overhead
records.fact: Kingfishers dive headfirst into the water with their eyes closed, aiming from memory at where the fish was a moment before.
records.role: A plunge-diving fish specialist. It watches from a perch, dives on small fish and crayfish, and then walks its catch back to a nest tunnel dug straight into a bare earth bank — no bank, no kingfishers, however many fish there are.

requirements.hint: Clear open water to dive into and a bare vertical earth bank to tunnel a nest into. A raised platform is the one thing a kingfisher will never use.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Belted Kingfisher life history

records.name: Green Heron
records.diet: Mainly small fish; also insects, crayfish and frogs
records.shelter: Loose stick nests on low branches leaning out over water
records.preferredHabitat: Quiet shady shallows under overhanging shrubs
records.fact: The green heron drops a feather, an insect or a scrap of bread onto the water as bait and waits for a fish to come and look — one of very few birds known to use tools.
records.role: A small, crafty heron of shady shallows and one of the few tool-using birds. It hunts from low branches right above the water, so it needs shrubby cover leaning out over the surface rather than tall timber.

requirements.hint: Low willow and alder leaning out over quiet water — the beaver's flooding is what creates it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Green Heron life history

records.name: Hooded Merganser
records.diet: Small fish, crayfish, dragonfly nymphs and other aquatic insects
records.shelter: Tree cavities in standing dead timber over or beside water
records.preferredHabitat: Quiet ponds with drowned standing trees
records.fact: Hooded merganser ducklings leap from a cavity up to fifteen metres above the ground the day after hatching and can dive for their own food within a day of landing.
records.role: A small diving duck with a serrated bill for gripping slippery prey and a third eyelid it uses as underwater goggles. It hunts fish, crayfish and insect nymphs below the surface and nests in cavities in drowned trees — which is why beaver ponds are its classic habitat.

requirements.hint: A beaver pond with dead standing trees in it. The cavities in drowned alder are where the hen nests — a box only works as a substitute.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Hooded Merganser life history
